paragraphs: It was little more than three-quarters of a mile from the town to the monastery. Alyosha walked quickly along the road, which was empty at that hour. It was almost night, and too dark to see anything clearly thirty paces ahead. Halfway there was a crossroads, and under a lone willow a figure came into view. As soon as Alyosha reached the crossroads, the figure stepped out and rushed at him, shouting savagely:
“Your money or your life!”
“So it’s you, Mitya,” cried Alyosha in surprise, though he was badly startled.

“Ha ha ha! You didn’t expect me? I wondered where to wait for you. By her house? There are three ways out of it, and I might have missed you. Then I thought, I’ll wait here, because you have to pass this spot, there’s no other way to the monastery. Come, tell me the truth. Crush me like a beetle. But what’s the matter?”

“Nothing, brother—it’s the fright you gave me. Oh, Dmitri! Father’s blood just now.” (Alyosha began to cry. He had been close to tears for a long time, and now something seemed to give way in his soul.) “You almost killed him—you cursed him—and now—here—you’re making jokes—‘Your money or your life!’”
“Well, what of it? It’s not decent—is that it? Not suitable for a man in my position?”
“No—I only—”

“Wait. Look at the night. See how dark it is, what clouds, what a wind has come up. I hid here under the willow, waiting for you. And as God is above, I suddenly thought: why go on suffering any longer, what is there to wait for? Here I have a willow, a handkerchief, a shirt. I can twist them into a rope in a minute, and my suspenders besides. Why go on burdening the earth and dishonoring it with my vile presence? And then I heard you coming—heavens, it was as though something flew down to me all at once. So there is a man I love after all. Here he is, my dear little brother, whom I love more than anyone in the world, the only one I love in the world. And I loved you so much, so much at that moment, that I thought, ‘I’ll throw my arms around his neck right now.’ Then a stupid idea hit me, to have a joke with you and scare you. I shouted, like a fool, ‘Your money!’ Forgive my foolery—it was only nonsense, and there’s nothing indecent in my soul.... Damn it all, tell me what happened. What did she say? Strike me, crush me, don’t spare me! Was she furious?”
“No, not that.... There was nothing like that, Mitya. There—I found them both there.”
“Both? Who?”
“Grushenka at Katerina Ivanovna’s.”
Dmitri was struck dumb.
“Impossible!” he cried. “You’re raving! Grushenka with her?”

Alyosha described everything that had happened from the moment he went into Katerina Ivanovna’s. It took him ten minutes to tell it. You couldn’t say he told it smoothly or in good order, but he seemed to make it clear, leaving out no important word or action and often conveying his own feelings vividly in a single word. Dmitri listened in silence, staring at him with a terrible fixed gaze, but Alyosha could see that he understood it all and had caught every point. As the story went on, though, his face grew not merely gloomy but menacing. He scowled and clenched his teeth, and his fixed stare became harder, more concentrated, more terrible still. Then suddenly, with incredible speed, his angry, savage face changed. His tightly pressed lips parted, and Dmitri Fyodorovitch burst into uncontrollable, spontaneous laughter. He literally shook with laughter. For a long time he could not speak.

“So she wouldn’t kiss her hand! So she didn’t kiss it; so she ran away!” he kept exclaiming in hysterical delight. You might have called it insolent delight, if it hadn’t been so spontaneous. “So the other one called her a tigress! And a tigress she is! So she ought to be flogged on a scaffold? Yes, yes, she ought. That’s just what I think. She ought to have been long ago. Here’s how it is, brother: let her be punished, but I have to get better first. I understand the queen of impudence. That’s her all over! You saw her whole self in that hand-kissing, the she-devil! She’s magnificent in her own line! So she ran home? I’ll go—ah—I’ll run to her! Alyosha, don’t blame me. I agree that hanging is too good for her.”
“But Katerina Ivanovna!” exclaimed Alyosha sorrowfully.

“I see her, too! I see right through her, as I never have before! It’s a real discovery of the four continents of the world, I mean the five! What a thing to do! That’s just like Katya, who wasn’t afraid to face a coarse, ill-mannered officer and risk a deadly insult, on a generous impulse to save her father! But the pride, the recklessness, the defiance of fate, the unbounded defiance! You say the aunt tried to stop her? That aunt, you know, is overbearing herself. She’s the sister of the general’s widow in Moscow, and even more stuck-up than she is. But her husband was caught stealing government money. He lost everything, his estate and all, and the proud wife had to lower her colors, and she hasn’t raised them since. So she tried to hold Katya back, but Katya wouldn’t listen! She thinks she can overcome anything, that everything will give way to her. She thought she could bewitch Grushenka if she liked, and she believed it herself. She plays a part to herself, and whose fault is that? Do you think she kissed Grushenka’s hand first on purpose, with a motive? No, she really was fascinated by Grushenka, that is, not by Grushenka, but by her own dream, her own delusion—because it was _her_ dream, _her_ delusion! Alyosha, darling, how did you get away from them, those women? Did you pick up your cassock and run? Ha ha ha!”

“Brother, you don’t seem to have noticed how you insulted Katerina Ivanovna by telling Grushenka about that day. And she threw it in her face just now, that she had gone secretly to gentlemen to sell her beauty! Brother, what could be worse than that insult?”
What worried Alyosha more than anything was that, incredible as it seemed, his brother appeared pleased by Katerina Ivanovna’s humiliation.

“Bah!” Dmitri frowned fiercely and struck his forehead with his hand. He had only now taken it in, though Alyosha had just told him of the insult and of Katerina Ivanovna’s cry: “Your brother is a scoundrel!”

“Yes, maybe I really did tell Grushenka about that ‘fatal day,’ as Katya calls it. Yes, I did tell her, I remember! It was that time at Mokroe. I was drunk, the gypsies were singing.... But I was sobbing. I was sobbing then, kneeling and praying to Katya’s image, and Grushenka understood. She understood it all then. I remember, she cried herself.... Damn it all! But it was bound to turn out like this.... Then she cried, but now it’s ‘the dagger in the heart’! That’s how women are.”
He looked down and sank into thought.

“Yes, I am a scoundrel, a complete scoundrel!” he said suddenly, in a gloomy voice. “It doesn’t matter whether I cried or not, I’m a scoundrel! Tell her I accept the name, if that’s any comfort to her. Come, that’s enough. Good-by. There’s no use talking! It’s not amusing. You go your way and I’ll go mine. And I don’t want to see you again, except as a last resort. Good-by, Alexey!”
He pressed Alyosha’s hand warmly and, still looking down, without raising his head, as though tearing himself away, turned quickly toward the town.
Alyosha looked after him, unable to believe he would go away so abruptly.

“Wait, Alexey, one more confession, to you alone!” cried Dmitri, suddenly turning back. “Look at me. Look at me well. You see here, here—a terrible disgrace is waiting for me.” (As he said “here,” Dmitri struck his chest with his fist, with a strange look, as though the dishonor lay exactly on his chest, in some spot, in a pocket perhaps, or hanging around his neck.) “You know me now: a scoundrel, an avowed scoundrel. But let me tell you that I have never done anything before, and never will again, that can compare in baseness with the dishonor I’m carrying at this very minute on my breast, here, here. It’s going to happen, though I’m perfectly free to stop it. I can stop it or carry it through, note that. Well, let me tell you, I’m going to carry it through. I won’t stop it. I told you everything just now, but I didn’t tell you this, because even I didn’t have the brass for it. I can still pull up. If I do, I can give back the full half of my lost honor tomorrow. But I won’t pull up. I’ll carry out my base plan, and you can bear witness that I told you so beforehand. Darkness and destruction! No need to explain. You’ll find out in due time. The filthy back alley and the she-devil. Good-by. Don’t pray for me, I’m not worth it. And there’s no need, no need at all.... I don’t need it! Away!”
And he suddenly walked off, this time for good. Alyosha went on toward the monastery.
“What? I’ll never see him again! What is he saying?” he wondered wildly. “Why, I’ll certainly see him tomorrow. I’ll look him up. I’ll make a point of it. What does he mean?”
He went around the monastery and crossed the pine wood to the hermitage. The door was opened to him, though no one was admitted at that hour. His heart trembled as he went into Father Zossima’s cell.

“Why, why had he gone out? Why had the elder sent him into the world? Here was peace. Here was holiness. But out there was confusion, there was darkness in which one lost one’s way and went astray at once....”

In the cell he found the novice Porfiry and Father Païssy, who came every hour to ask after Father Zossima. Alyosha learned with alarm that the elder was getting worse and worse. Even his usual talk with the brothers could not take place that day. As a rule, every evening after the service the monks crowded into Father Zossima’s cell, and each confessed aloud his sins of the day, his sinful thoughts and temptations, even his quarrels, if there had been any. Some confessed kneeling. The elder absolved, reconciled, exhorted, imposed penance, blessed, and dismissed them. It was against this general “confession” that the opponents of “elders” protested. They maintained that it was a profanation of the sacrament of confession, almost a sacrilege, though this was quite a different thing. They even told the diocesan authorities that such confessions did no good, and in fact led, to a large extent, to sin and temptation. Many of the brothers disliked going to the elder, and went against their will, because everyone went, and for fear of being accused of pride and rebellious ideas. People said that some of the monks agreed beforehand, saying, “I’ll confess that I lost my temper with you this morning, and you back me up,” simply so that they would have something to say. Alyosha knew that this really did happen sometimes. He knew, too, that some of the monks deeply resented the custom of taking letters from relatives to the elder, to be opened and read by him before they reached the people they were addressed to.

It was assumed, of course, that all this was done freely and in good faith, as voluntary submission and wholesome guidance. But in fact there was sometimes a good deal of insincerity, and much that was false and forced in the practice. Yet the older and more experienced monks held to their opinion. They argued that “for those who have come within these walls sincerely seeking salvation, such obedience and sacrifice will certainly be wholesome and of great benefit. Those who find it irksome and complain are no true monks, and have made a mistake in entering the monastery—their proper place is in the world. Even in the temple one cannot be safe from sin and the devil. So there was no use taking it too much into account.”

“He is weaker, a drowsiness has come over him,” Father Païssy whispered to Alyosha as he blessed him. “It’s hard to rouse him. And he must not be roused. He woke for five minutes, sent his blessing to the brothers, and asked for their prayers for him tonight. He intends to take the sacrament again in the morning. He remembered you, Alexey. He asked whether you had gone away, and was told that you were in the town. ‘I blessed him for that work,’ he said. ‘His place is there, not here, for a while.’ Those were his words about you. He remembered you lovingly, with concern. Do you understand how he honored you? But why has he decided that you should spend some time in the world? He must have foreseen something in your destiny! Understand this, Alexey: if you return to the world, it must be to do the duty laid on you by your elder, and not for frivolous vanity and worldly pleasures.”

Father Païssy went out. Alyosha had no doubt that Father Zossima was dying, though he might live another day or two. Alyosha resolved, firmly and ardently, that in spite of his promises to his father, the Hohlakovs and Katerina Ivanovna, he would not leave the monastery the next day, but would stay with his elder to the end. His heart glowed with love, and he bitterly reproached himself for having been able, even for one moment, to forget the man he had left in the monastery on his deathbed, the man he honored above everyone in the world. He went into Father Zossima’s bedroom, knelt down, and bowed to the ground before the elder, who slept quietly without stirring, breathing evenly and hardly audibly, with a peaceful face.

Alyosha went back to the other room, where Father Zossima had received his guests in the morning. Taking off his boots, he lay down on the hard, narrow leather sofa, which he had long used as a bed, bringing nothing but a pillow. The mattress his father had shouted to him about that morning, he had long forgotten to lie on. He took off his cassock and used it as a blanket. But before going to bed, he fell on his knees and prayed for a long time. In his fervent prayer he did not ask God to lighten his darkness. He only thirsted for the joyful feeling that always visited his soul after the praise and adoration of which his evening prayer usually consisted. That joy always brought him light, untroubled sleep. As he was praying, he suddenly felt in his pocket the little pink note the servant had handed him as he left Katerina Ivanovna’s. He was disturbed, but he finished his prayer. Then, after some hesitation, he opened the envelope. In it was a letter to him, signed by Lise, the young daughter of Madame Hohlakov, who had laughed at him in front of the elder that morning.

“Alexey Fyodorovitch,” she wrote, “I’m writing to you without anyone’s knowing, not even mamma, and I know how wrong it is. But I can’t live without telling you the feeling that has sprung up in my heart, and no one but the two of us must know it for a while. But how am I to say what I want so much to tell you? They say paper doesn’t blush, but I assure you that’s not true, and it’s blushing just as I am now, all over. Dear Alyosha, I love you. I’ve loved you since I was a child, since our Moscow days, when you were very different from what you are now, and I shall love you all my life. My heart has chosen you, so that we can join our lives and spend them together until we’re old. Of course, on condition that you leave the monastery. As for our age, we will wait until the time the law fixes. By then I’ll certainly be quite strong, I’ll be walking and dancing. There can be no doubt of that.

“You see how I’ve thought of everything. There’s only one thing I can’t imagine: what you’ll think of me when you read this. I’m always laughing and being naughty. I made you angry this morning, but I assure you that before I picked up my pen, I prayed before the Image of the Mother of God, and now I’m praying, and almost crying.

“My secret is in your hands. When you come tomorrow, I don’t know how I’ll look at you. Ah, Alexey Fyodorovitch, what if I can’t stop myself and laugh like a silly when I look at you, as I did today? You’ll think I’m a nasty girl making fun of you, and you won’t believe my letter. And so I beg you, dear one, if you have any pity for me, when you come tomorrow, don’t look me straight in the face, because if I meet your eyes, it’s sure to make me laugh, especially since you’ll be in that long gown. I feel cold all over when I think of it, so when you come, don’t look at me at all for a while, look at mamma or at the window....

“Here I’ve written you a love letter. Oh, dear, what have I done? Alyosha, don’t despise me, and if I’ve done something very horrid and hurt you, forgive me. Now the secret of my reputation, ruined perhaps for ever, is in your hands.
“I shall certainly cry today. Good-by until we meet, our _awful_ meeting.—LISE.
“P.S.—Alyosha! You must, must, must come!—LISE.”

Alyosha read the note in amazement, read it through twice, thought for a little, and suddenly laughed a soft, sweet laugh. He started. That laugh seemed sinful to him. But a minute later he laughed again, just as softly and happily. He slowly put the note back in the envelope, crossed himself and lay down. The turmoil in his heart passed at once. “God, have mercy on all of them. Keep all these unhappy and restless souls in Your care, and set them on the right path. All ways are Yours. Save them according to Your wisdom. You are love. You will send joy to all!” Alyosha murmured, crossing himself, and fell into peaceful sleep.
